titleStmt.title: Memorandum From Secretary of State Shultz to President Reagan

div.head: 386. Memorandum From Secretary of State Shultz to President Reagan

list.label: SUBJECT
list.item: State Visit of Ecuadorean President Leon Febres-Cordero

div.p: I. WHERE DOES OUR RELATIONSHIP STAND?

list.item: Very close since August 1984 inauguration of conservative, businessman/President Febres-Cordero.
We helped preserve civilian rule under previous GOE administration, and to this one we stress our commitment to the process and practice of democracy.
As promised in his June 1984 meeting with you, Febres-Cordero has pursued market based, growth oriented policies.

Febres-Cordero agrees with us on Central America, narcotics and terrorism. —
He broke relations with Nicaragua in October after exchanging harsh words with Ortega. —
He has taken a tough posture against narcotics traffickers and an increasingly dangerous local terrorist group.
That democracy grow stronger. Febres-Cordero has given questionable interpretations to an admittedly ambiguous constitution. He needs to be reminded of our concern for strong democratic institutions.
That Febres-Cordero’s free market approach succeed.
That the Alfaro Vive, Carajo! (AVC) terrorists be defeated.

Anxious to have visible and tangible US support. This State Visit will play well at home. Our record of assistance gives substance to our words of support. —
But, given his close affinity with us, Febres Cordero expresses surprise that our aid has not come more rapidly and in greater quantity. —
He has asked for PL 480 Title I to help continue agricultural sector reforms begun with the FY 85 Title I program. OMB and Treasury are resisting.

Participation in the U.S. Program for Sustained Growth. Ecuador follows most of the policies we support for debt management and growth. —
Febres-Cordero will host a working breakfast for Secretary Baker, Chairman Volcker, myself and heads of international financial institutions in pursuit of this goal.

div.p: IV. WHAT CAN BE ACHIEVED FROM THIS VISIT?

list.item: A re-emphasis of US support for the consolidation of democratic institutions and practices in Ecuador.
Praise for a small South American country’s courageous effort to implement its market based philosophy in a region long addicted to statist solutions.

A sharp contrast between Ecuador, a democracy with a solid market based economic program and a good human rights record, and Nicaragua, a totalitarian state with growing state control of its economy. —
Febres-Cordero publicly denigrated the Sandinistas for not holding free elections. Ortega’s critical retort led to Febres-Cordero breaking relations.

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Trip File, Trip Book for Brazil (Tillman) 2/23/1986–02/26/1986 (1). Secret.

In telegram 31956 to Quito, January 31, the Department reported on the January 15 breakfast hosted by Febres-Cordero for Shultz, Baker, Volcker, the IMF and IDB Presidents, and the IBRD Acting President, noting “Secretary Shultz said the Ecuadorean program is bound to be successful and Secretary Baker said those present could help encourage a return to voluntary commercial lending.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D860081–0481) In a January 15 memorandum to Reagan, Shultz described the meeting, writing that “Febres-Cordero demonstrated clearly that Ecuador is a country that has already adopted the type of economic program we have been urging on debtor countries. The breakfast meeting will underscore publicly our private support for Febres-Cordero’s efforts to get the commercial banks to renew voluntary lending.” (Reagan Library, George P. Shultz Papers, Box 33, President’s Evening Reading January–March 1986)
